claims.claim_text: Firms consume not quotes but a fitted implied-volatility surface, from which prices, Greeks, and risk-neutral densities are derived (Fengler, 2009)<!--ref:S2--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->.

On a single date, call prices must be non-increasing and convex in strike, total variance must not decrease with maturity, and the zero-maturity limit must match intrinsic value (Gatheral & Jacquier, 2013<!--ref:S1--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->; Guo et al., 2016)<!--ref:P1--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->.
Across dates, no self-financing strategy in the option panel may produce a riskless profit (Niu, 2015 [preprint])<!--ref:C2--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->.
Construction is therefore constrained estimation rather than interpolation, run at scale on dense, noisy quotes (Wiedemann et al., 2025)<!--ref:N2--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->.

A method may be arbitrage-free because its parameter domain excludes violations (Guo et al., 2016)<!--ref:P1--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->, because a penalty discourages them (Na et al., 2023 [preprint])<!--ref:N5--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->, because a post-fit map removes them (Bender & Thiel, 2020)<!--ref:R3--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->, or because a generator is screened before output (Bajalica et al., 2026)<!--ref:G5--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->.

The literature rarely separates them, and uses the same phrase for the static condition and for the dynamic one, although the second concerns the joint law of a surface process rather than the admissibility of one surface (Niu, 2015)<!--ref:C2--><!--anchor:section:1.1-->.

One disclosed exception is retained: a single-stock panel (Stahl & Blauth, 2024)<!--ref:C5--><!--anchor:section:1.3-->, admitted because it tests a martingale-defect condition directly, is scope-flagged throughout, and is never generalised to index surfaces.

A surface is statically admissible if, expressed through the normalised call price $c(k,\tau)=C/F_{\tau}$, it satisfies five conditions: **SC1**, non-negative time value, $c(k,\tau)\ge\max(1-e^{k},0)$; **SC2**, monotone decreasing call prices in strike, $\partial c/\partial k\le 0$; **SC3**, strike convexity, the butterfly or Durrleman condition, $\partial^{2} c/\partial k^{2}\ge 0$; **SC4**, the zero-maturity limit $c(\cdot,0)=\max(1-e^{k},0)$; and **SC5**, calendar monotonicity of total variance, $w$ non-decreasing in $\tau$ (Anagha, 2026 [preprint]; Gatheral & Jacquier, 2013<!--ref:S1--><!--anchor:section:2.1-->; Martini & Mingone, 2022<!--ref:P2--><!--anchor:section:2.1-->)<!--ref:G6--><!--anchor:section:2.1-->.

Gatheral and Jacquier (2013)<!--ref:S1--><!--anchor:section:2.1--> give closed-form **sufficient** conditions on the raw stochastic-volatility-inspired (SVI) parameters that guarantee SC1–SC4 on each slice, with a separate condition for SC5.

Martini and Mingone (2022)<!--ref:P2--><!--anchor:section:2.1--> establish a characterisation that is **exact** for the SVI slice, expressed through monotonicity of the quantities $-d_{1}$ and $-d_{2}$ rather than through a restricted parameter box.
(2016)<!--ref:P1--><!--anchor:section:2.1--> generalise the family and show that arbitrage-free surfaces exist outside the SVI class, with the guarantee carried by the parameter domain itself.

The canonical failure is instructive: the SABR (stochastic alpha, beta, rho) implied-volatility approximation admits negative implied densities at low strikes for long maturities, a finite-strike violation that required a one-dimensional partial-differential-equation (PDE) density fix (Hagan et al., 2014)<!--ref:S3--><!--anchor:section:2.1-->.

Asymptotic statements sit on the other side of the same distinction: a family can be asymptotically arbitrage-free in the wings while violating a condition at the strikes a desk actually quotes (Fukasawa, 2022)<!--ref:C4--><!--anchor:section:2.1-->.

Operationally, the corpus's conditions are exercised by repair and generation rows as well as by parametric ones (Bajalica et al., 2026; Xiong & Liu, 2026<!--ref:R5--><!--anchor:section:2.1-->)<!--ref:G5--><!--anchor:section:2.1-->, which is why SC1–SC5 serve as the review's static predicate rather than as a description of one family.

A dynamic condition constrains a family of surfaces indexed by calendar time, and the natural formulation is a filtered probability space on which the option-price process is a martingale under a measure consistent with the numéraire (Niu, 2015)<!--ref:C2--><!--anchor:section:2.2-->.
One review of static and dynamic conditions discusses the question without testing it (Niu, 2015)<!--ref:C2--><!--anchor:section:2.2-->.

A neural stochastic-differential-equation (SDE) market model constructs a state space of statically arbitrage-free prices and explicitly limits its claim to static, model-independent admissibility (Cohen et al., 2021)<!--ref:G7--><!--anchor:section:2.2-->.

A path-dependent construction builds surfaces along stochastic paths that are statically free but does not test dynamic consistency across the resulting family (Andrès et al., 2026)<!--ref:C3--><!--anchor:section:2.2-->.

A parametric family reports time-indexed arbitrage probabilities, which is a statement about a model's parameters over time rather than a path-level test of the fitted surface (Barski & Wiśniewolski, 2026 [preprint])<!--ref:P8--><!--anchor:section:2.2-->.
A single-stock panel examines martingale defects and bubble conditions and is dynamic-adjacent, but it is scope-flagged (Stahl & Blauth, 2024)<!--ref:C5--><!--anchor:section:2.2-->.

Two rows construct by distorting a reference function and also repair an existing quote set, so they sit between construction and repair (Bender & Thiel, 2020<!--ref:R3--><!--anchor:section:2.3-->; Buehler et al., 2026 [preprint])<!--ref:R6--><!--anchor:section:2.3-->.
One row's constraint is architectural rather than a penalty term, which makes it a hybrid (Cao et al., 2020)<!--ref:N1--><!--anchor:section:2.3-->.

Two constructions are model-level rather than data-driven, so their guarantee is inherited from the model class (Andrès et al., 2026; Cohen et al., 2021<!--ref:G7--><!--anchor:section:2.3-->)<!--ref:C3--><!--anchor:section:2.3-->.

Abstract coverage is uneven: 34 abstracts were read in full, four only partially (R2, G3, C4, S1), and three were unavailable, leaving those rows at title level (P4, P7, R4).

Within-study baselines are the only licensed comparisons: a hard-constrained generator against surface SVI (SSVI) and a soft-penalty network (Anagha, 2026)<!--ref:G6--><!--anchor:section:3.3-->, a generative adversarial network (GAN) against a variational autoencoder (Sidogi et al., 2022)<!--ref:N4--><!--anchor:section:3.3-->, a penalty model against an artificial neural network (Na et al., 2023)<!--ref:N5--><!--anchor:section:3.3-->, and a repair procedure across five completion backends (Xiong & Liu, 2026)<!--ref:R5--><!--anchor:section:3.3-->.

The clearest case is a generalised SVI family whose arbitrage-freeness is inherited from the structure of the parameter set, with the guarantee holding for all admitted parameters rather than only at the fitted optimum (Guo et al., 2016)<!--ref:P1--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->.

A second line replaces a sufficient parameter box with an exact butterfly characterisation, so that the admissible set is not narrower than necessary and calibration proceeds on the true admissible region (Martini & Mingone, 2022)<!--ref:P2--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->.

A third extends the construction across maturities jointly, calibrating an extended SSVI parameterisation as one object rather than slice by slice, so that calendar monotonicity is a property of the joint fit (Mingone, 2022)<!--ref:P3--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->.
A sequential slice-wise counterpart reaches the same family by a different route, available here only at title level (Corbetta et al., 2019)<!--ref:P4--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->.

A random-coefficient parameterisation widens the set of shapes the family can represent, including bimodal short-dated densities that fixed-coefficient forms cannot produce, while retaining a structural guarantee (Zaugg et al., 2025)<!--ref:P5--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->.

A class-C3 interpolation constructs from a smaller knot set rather than calibrating to quotes, which changes what the guarantee is a claim about: the interpolant is admissible by construction, and the fit to data is a separate question (Le Floc’h, 2025)<!--ref:P6--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->.

A bounded-factor model derives conditions under which the implied surface of a Gaussian-factor structure is free of static arbitrage and reports time-indexed arbitrage probabilities; it is the only parametric row that reports anything indexed by time (Barski & Wiśniewolski, 2026)<!--ref:P8--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->.
A further row claims necessary-and-sufficient conditions for the SSVI/S3 curve but is metadata-only here and cannot corroborate them (Klassen, 2016 [preprint])<!--ref:P7--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->.

An interpolation-by-distortion that begins from an arbitrage-free reference and a linear-programming construction both embed the constraint in a deterministic construction, yet what they certify is a transformed object rather than an admitted parameter vector (Bender & Thiel, 2020<!--ref:R3--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->; Buehler et al., 2026)<!--ref:R6--><!--anchor:section:4.1-->.

The clearest architectural case is a gated network whose slopes and weights are constructed so that the option-price function is frictionless and convex by design; the gate is a constraint-bearing architecture, so the row sits on the penalty/architectural boundary (Cao et al., 2020)<!--ref:N1--><!--anchor:section:4.2-->.

A graph neural operator is trained across a ten-year intraday S&P 500 index (SPX) panel and reports adherence without a stated tolerance, which makes the claim hard to audit (Wiedemann et al., 2025)<!--ref:N2--><!--anchor:section:4.2-->.

A deep-smoothing approach adds soft penalties plus a plug-in correction, aimed at sparse and erroneous quotes, and the penalty is not a guarantee (Ackerer et al., 2019 [preprint])<!--ref:N3--><!--anchor:section:4.2-->.

A GAN with a static-arbitrage loss on the FTSE/JSE All Share (ALSI) index states plainly that the condition cannot be directly learned through the penalty route, which is the most explicit statement in the corpus of what a penalty can and cannot deliver (Sidogi et al., 2022)<!--ref:N4--><!--anchor:section:4.2-->.

A second penalty model minimises violations and compares accuracy and runtime against an artificial neural network, reporting a residual rather than a certificate (Na et al., 2023)<!--ref:N5--><!--anchor:section:4.2-->.

A deep convolutional network embeds derivative constraints, including a maturity-derivative term, in the loss and trains on SABR-generated data, so its reported adherence is an in-sample property of a simulated generator (Hoshisashi et al., 2023 [preprint])<!--ref:N6--><!--anchor:section:4.2-->.

One row is a hybrid: a gated network's constraint is structural rather than a soft term, so it is flagged and not used to support either claim alone (Cao et al., 2020)<!--ref:N1--><!--anchor:section:4.2-->.

The projection line is represented by a linear-programming repair that moves prices minimally inside the bid–ask without any cross-date enforcement claim (Cohen et al., 2020)<!--ref:R1--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->, and by an entropic projection to the arbitrage-free set built on Sinkhorn's algorithm, whose convergence proof is a proof about the projection (De March & Henry-Labordère, 2019 [preprint])<!--ref:R2--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->.

A third line begins from an arbitrage-free reference function and distorts it, so the construction and the repair share the same observable; the Kahalé approach appears as a special case (Bender & Thiel, 2020)<!--ref:R3--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->.

A strictly arbitrage-free non-parametric construction calibrates by linear programming with a positive discrete local volatility, which places it at the construction edge of the repair locus (Buehler et al., 2026)<!--ref:R6--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->.

An observation-anchored repair runs over 252 out-of-sample SPX days and five completion backends and reports a butterfly violation floor of about 5.4%, so the repaired surface is not violation-free on real quotes; a cubic-spline backend has the lowest reconstruction error after repair (Xiong & Liu, 2026)<!--ref:R5--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->.

A Chebyshev-tensor surface with a quadratic-programming stage and a post-fit adjustment reports under 1% static violations and 98–99% inside-spread coverage in calm years, with out-of-band leakage under stress (Alvarez, 2025 [preprint])<!--ref:R7--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->.

A Markov-chain approximation over 2,695 SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) options across 28 maturities carries a time axis without a dynamic audit (Madan & Schoutens, 2019)<!--ref:R9--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->.

One row asserts transformations without either proof or test (Zetocha, 2023 [preprint])<!--ref:R8--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->, and another expands the scope to joint American call-and-put smoothing at title level (Yao et al., 2026)<!--ref:R4--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->.

The family's baseline is the shape-constrained smoothing spline, which showed that ignoring the constraint matters, before the four-family split existed (Fengler, 2009)<!--ref:S2--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->.

Two earlier constructions did not enforce admissibility at all: a nonparametric inversion solved for a surface without an explicit constraint set (Bodurtha & Jermakyan, 1999)<!--ref:S4--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->, and a semiparametric factor model on DAX (Deutscher Aktienindex) data estimated dynamics without enforcement (Fengler et al., 2006)<!--ref:S5--><!--anchor:section:4.3-->.

A variational autoencoder over the parameters of stochastic-volatility models generates surfaces whose admissibility follows from the SDE class rather than from the training objective (Ning et al., 2023)<!--ref:G1--><!--anchor:section:4.4-->.
A neural-SDE state space defines a family of statically arbitrage-free prices and explicitly disclaims a dynamic guarantee (Cohen et al., 2021)<!--ref:G7--><!--anchor:section:4.4-->.
A gated rational network is arbitrage-free by design, one of the earliest architectural guarantees in the corpus (Yang et al., 2017)<!--ref:G8--><!--anchor:section:4.4-->.

Trainable hard constraints go further: the constraint is imposed as a differentiable but hard architectural element, and the row reports 0.00% violations at a $10^{-4}$ tolerance over 15 runs on synthetic SVI data (Anagha, 2026)<!--ref:G6--><!--anchor:section:4.4-->.

A VolGAN (a volatility GAN) generates joint surface and underlying scenarios and evaluates them through hedging against a Black–Scholes delta, while the enforcement mechanism is not described (Vuletić & Cont, 2024)<!--ref:G2--><!--anchor:section:4.4-->.
A simulation approach places static constraints inside a generated process but is only partly available at abstract level (Cont & Vuletić, 2023)<!--ref:G3--><!--anchor:section:4.4-->.

A GAN denoiser reports lower mean-squared error (MSE) and runtime without a guarantee claim, which makes it a smoothing tool rather than a certified generator (Ginart Belmonte & Cole, 2025)<!--ref:G4--><!--anchor:section:4.4-->.

A latent flow-matching generator reports that 90.8% of generated surfaces pass all tested static conditions, the corpus's clearest pass-rate statement (Bajalica et al., 2026)<!--ref:G5--><!--anchor:section:4.4-->.

Six rows audit their own output: a graph neural operator reporting adherence on ten years of intraday data (Wiedemann et al., 2025)<!--ref:N2--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->, a deep network with derivative constraints on simulated data (Hoshisashi et al., 2023)<!--ref:N6--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->, a repair reporting a 5.4% butterfly floor (Xiong & Liu, 2026)<!--ref:R5--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->, a Chebyshev construction reporting under 1% violations (Alvarez, 2025)<!--ref:R7--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->, a flow-matching generator reporting a 90.8% pass rate (Bajalica et al., 2026)<!--ref:G5--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->, and a hard-constrained generator reporting 0.00% at $10^{-4}$ over 15 runs (Anagha, 2026)<!--ref:G6--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->.

H2 is unsupported in its fit-error clause — no penalty or repair row reports a lower fit error than a constrained parametric baseline on the same data, and the one paired measurement reports a higher error for the stronger guarantee — while its burden-displacement clause is supported: weights, tolerances, repair steps, and acceptance thresholds are where the constraint work is absorbed (Na et al., 2023<!--ref:N5--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->; Sidogi et al., 2022<!--ref:N4--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->; Xiong & Liu, 2026)<!--ref:R5--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->.

H3 is supported for the penalised-sampling branch, where a pass rate is the whole claim, and disconfirmed for the inherited-guarantee branch, where four rows are structural rather than sample-filtered (Anagha, 2026<!--ref:G6--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->; Cohen et al., 2021<!--ref:G7--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->; Ning et al., 2023<!--ref:G1--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->; Yang et al., 2017)<!--ref:G8--><!--anchor:section:5.1-->.
Preprints are labelled wherever cited, so a reader can see that three of the six audit rows are preprints (N6, R7, G6).

A hard-constrained generator is compared with SSVI and a soft-penalty network on the same data (Anagha, 2026)<!--ref:G6--><!--anchor:section:5.2-->; a GAN with a variational autoencoder (Sidogi et al., 2022)<!--ref:N4--><!--anchor:section:5.2-->; a penalty model with an artificial neural network (Na et al., 2023)<!--ref:N5--><!--anchor:section:5.2-->; and a repair procedure across five completion backends (Xiong & Liu, 2026)<!--ref:R5--><!--anchor:section:5.2-->.

A neural detector of model-free static arbitrage exists as an independent auditor, but it is never applied to another row in this corpus (Neufeld & Sester, 2024)<!--ref:C1--><!--anchor:section:5.2-->.
A hard-constrained generator reports a structural guarantee and a 0.00% audit, and also reports a higher total-variance error than two baselines (Anagha, 2026)<!--ref:G6--><!--anchor:section:5.3-->.
A repair reports a 5.4% floor and selects a backend by reconstruction error (Xiong & Liu, 2026)<!--ref:R5--><!--anchor:section:5.3-->.
A Chebyshev construction reports sub-1% violations and inside-spread coverage with stressed-year leakage (Alvarez, 2025)<!--ref:R7--><!--anchor:section:5.3-->.
A flow-matching generator reports a pass rate without a paired fit-cost comparison (Bajalica et al., 2026)<!--ref:G5--><!--anchor:section:5.3-->.
The one row that reports all three does so on synthetic data (Anagha, 2026)<!--ref:G6--><!--anchor:section:6.1-->, which shows that the triple is reportable rather than idealised.

The two penalty rows that concede the limit of their route are the clearest evidence that the authors know which claim they are making (Na et al., 2023; Sidogi et al., 2022<!--ref:N4--><!--anchor:section:6.1-->)<!--ref:N5--><!--anchor:section:6.1-->.

To our knowledge, based on searches of OpenAlex covering 2015-01-01 to 2026-11-23, as of 2026-11-23 no included study states and tests a process-level dynamic no-arbitrage condition for an equity-index implied-volatility surface; the nearest prior work reviews the conditions without testing them (Niu, 2015)<!--ref:C2--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->.

A generator that constrains maturity monotonicity has made a static claim (Anagha, 2026<!--ref:G6--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->; Bajalica et al., 2026<!--ref:G5--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->), as has a repair that enforces it (Xiong & Liu, 2026)<!--ref:R5--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->.

The neural-SDE row explicitly disclaims dynamics (Cohen et al., 2021)<!--ref:G7--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->; the one review that treats dynamic conditions at length does not test them (Niu, 2015)<!--ref:C2--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->; and the path-dependent and time-indexed constructions build objects along a time axis without a process-level test (Andrès et al., 2026<!--ref:C3--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->; Barski & Wiśniewolski, 2026)<!--ref:P8--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->.

A finite-strike SABR failure and an asymptotic arbitrage-free approximation are compatible statements because they hold in different regimes: the first says a quoted surface admits a negative density at long maturities, the second says the wings behave correctly as strikes grow (Fukasawa, 2022; Hagan et al., 2014<!--ref:S3--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->)<!--ref:C4--><!--anchor:section:6.2-->.

Starting from a surface family with a stated process (Andrès et al., 2026<!--ref:C3--><!--anchor:section:6.3-->; Barski & Wiśniewolski, 2026)<!--ref:P8--><!--anchor:section:6.3-->, it would define a path-level admissibility condition and run it over a multi-year index panel.

The third is a residual audit for proof constructions: applying an independent detector (Neufeld & Sester, 2024)<!--ref:C1--><!--anchor:section:6.3--> to proof-bearing parametric and repair rows would test whether their guarantees survive finite-sample implementation, reporting violations at a stated tolerance on observed quotes.

The fourth is a test-power and noise-floor study, which would estimate false-positive and false-negative rates of violation tests and separate data noise from method error; the 5.4% repair floor is the motivating case (Xiong & Liu, 2026)<!--ref:R5--><!--anchor:section:6.3-->.

R3 is a repair built on an admissible reference function, so its mechanism is closer to construction; it stays in R because the manuscript's repair locus is defined by the certified object, and R3 certifies its output.
R6 claims a strict guarantee through parameter positivity, which is architecturally parametric, but its object is a completed surface, and it anchors the repair family's strict end.
G7 satisfies its constraints on a modelled state space and explicitly disclaims a dynamic-arbitrage guarantee, which is why it marks the static/dynamic boundary rather than a gap in it.

The corpus is 41 sources — 36 published in 2015–2026 and 5 seminal precursors — of which 29 are peer-reviewed and 11 are preprints, coded on eight fields and read at abstract level; no systematic-review compliance or method ranking is claimed.
Seventeen sources assert their guarantee at proof level, 16 report a numerical test, and 8 assert admissibility with neither.
As reported in the abstracts, the certified object in all 41 rows is a single date's surface, and no source enforces or tests dynamic no-arbitrage, including none of the 31 construction rows.
Proof-level and test-level evidence come from almost disjoint sets, and no two sources state data, metric and tolerance together, so no two rows are directly comparable.

Because the surface is what prices, hedges, and clears, a fitted artefact that admits arbitrage can in principle propagate into risk numbers, margin, and capital; that propagation is a premise, not a measurement: no study in this corpus tests it.
The corpus contains no such test.
Ten rows engage time; none states a path-level condition and checks it over a path.
Retrieval requested 775 records and returned 750.
One query ("SVI stochastic volatility inspired") was lost after a Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) 429 response; 21 first-pass responses were rate-limited and 20 were recovered on retry.
De-duplication left 430 unique records.

Screening excluded 389 under eight reason codes: off-topic (141), pre-2015 background (86), relevant but not selected (40), out-of-scope asset class (34), publication type (32), duplicate version (31), forecasting or trading (21), and model-calibration pricing (4).

Forty-one studies were included: 36 in-window records and five declared seminal precursors dated 1999–2014, comprising 29 peer-reviewed articles or proceedings papers, 11 preprints (26.8%), and one practitioner magazine article.
All 41 records were resolved to a DOI-bearing index record (41/41); no record was flagged retracted by the OpenAlex `is_retracted` field.
Evidence is abstract-level: 34 records were read in full abstract, four only partially, and three at title level, so every claim about what a study did is a claim about what its abstract reports.
The corpus splits into 17 proof-level rows, 16 numerical tests, and 8 assumptions; within the 36 in-window records the split is 16 / 14 / 6, and the five seminal precursors contribute 1 / 2 / 2.
